classic-mixed-vegetables-frozen-cooked-w.title: Classic Mixed Vegetables, Frozen, Cooked with Butter or Margarine

content.title: About
content.content: A classic frozen vegetable mix (broccoli, carrots, cauliflower, peas) prepared with butter or margarine. The vegetables heat quickly, retain bright colour, a crisp texture and a characteristic buttery flavour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables are flash‑frozen right after harvest, preserving most of their vitamins and minerals.
Butter gives a rich aroma, while margarine provides a more neutral taste and a longer shelf life.
The mix is a staple in school cafeterias and a convenient side dish for home cooking.
Quick thermal processing retains antioxidants such as carotenoids in carrots and vitamin C in broccoli.
Packaging is usually multi‑layered to protect against moisture and light.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Source of dietary fibre
items.content: Fibre aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps maintain healthy blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene, vitamin C and other antioxidants help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin K found in broccoli and cauliflower contribute to bone strength.

items.title: Low‑calorie option
items.content: Vegetables have a low energy density, making them suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions are lightly salted; people monitoring salt intake should check the label.

items.title: Trans fats in margarine
items.content: If margarine is used, it may contain trans fats, which should be limited.

items.title: Vitamin loss over time
items.content: Prolonged freezer storage can reduce certain vitamins, especially vitamin C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the mix in the microwave or in a skillet, adding a little extra butter if needed. Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or incorporate into quick‑prep meals. Season with herbs, garlic or soy sauce for extra flavour.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, use within 3–4 months. Do not thaw and refreeze, as quality may deteriorate.

content.title: About
content.content: Kale (Brassica oleracea var. sabellica) is a leafy vegetable known for its high levels of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. When boiled (about 5‑7 minutes) most nutrients are retained and the texture becomes tender, making it suitable for soups, purees, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kale is often called a “superfood” because of its dense nutrient profile.
Ancient Roman varieties were cultivated, and it became popular throughout medieval Europe.
Leaves can be green, purple, or variegated depending on the cultivar.
Kale is frost‑tolerant and can continue growing in sub‑zero temperatures.
In Japan, kale is known as “katsuka” and is used in traditional dishes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Kale provides over 700% of the daily value for vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Abundant antioxidants
items.content: Kale contains carotenoids, quercetin, and other polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of calcium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for bone, muscle, and nerve function.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein and fiber
items.content: Kale contributes plant protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and digestive health.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High vitamin K intake may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Kale contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled kale can be added to soups, stews, salads, served as a side dish with meat or fish, or blended into a puree. Before cooking, rinse the leaves well and remove thick stems.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh kale in the refrigerator in a bag or container with a slight moisture for up to 5 days. Cooked kale should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Lemon (Citrus × limon) is a bright yellow citrus fruit with a sour, acidic juice and an aromatic, oil-rich peel. It is thought to have originated in northeastern India, Myanmar, and China. Lemons are used in drinks, cooking, baking, marinades, and dressings, and their zest adds fragrance and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lemon is a hybrid between citron and bitter orange.
Lemon juice is very acidic because of its high citric acid content.
Sailors once carried lemons and limes on long voyages to prevent scurvy, a vitamin C deficiency disease.
The peel contains aromatic oils that are used for flavoring and in cleaning and perfume products.
Preserved lemons, made with salt, are used in North African cooking.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Lemons provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Lemons contain plant compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Adds flavor without salt
items.content: Lemon juice and zest can brighten the flavor of food and reduce the need for added salt.

items.title: Contains citric acid
items.content: Citric acid in lemon juice may help reduce the risk of some kidney stones in some people, although more research is needed.

items.title: Provides hydration
items.content: Adding lemon to water can make drinking water more appealing.

items.title: Tooth enamel
items.content: The acid in lemon juice can wear down tooth enamel. Dilute juice, drink it with a straw, and rinse your mouth with water afterward.

items.title: Heartburn
items.content: Lemon may trigger heartburn or reflux in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Skin sensitivity
items.content: Lemon juice on the skin followed by sun exposure can cause irritation or a burn-like reaction.

items.title: Allergic reactions and mouth sores
items.content: Some people may be allergic to citrus, and lemon can irritate mouth sores.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lemon juice can be squeezed into water, tea, dressings, marinades, sauces, and baked goods, and over fish, vegetables, and salads. The zest adds flavor to baking, pasta, and dressings. Use the zest of unwaxed lemons, washed well.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store lemons at room temperature for about a week or in the refrigerator for several weeks. Lemon juice can be frozen in ice cube trays. Keep cut lemons in an airtight container in the refrigerator and use them within a few days.
